markdownRemark.html:
In Exposure vs Brightness I measured what the Exposure and Brightness sliders do to a pixel. Along the way I wrote that a pixel is three numbers from 0 to 255, and then added a throwaway line about a “Pandora’s box of color profiles and color spaces” that I couldn’t close again. This is me opening the box.

The question I should have asked first is a simple one: what does 255 · 0 · 0 actually mean? Everything below follows from it:

  • What is a color space? Is sRGB one? What does the “s” stand for?
  • Why can the same three numbers be two different colors?
  • If a screen can’t show a color, why not just use more bits?

The one idea to keep in your pocket: 255 · 0 · 0 is not a color. It is an instruction (“turn the red light all the way up”), and which red you get depends on who receives it.

The color series: 1. What an RGB number actually means (you are here) · 2. Where the horseshoe comes from · 3. HSL and HSV: RGB with different knobs · 4. Lab: numbers that match what you see · 5. Why gradients go muddy

Disclaimer: I’m learning color by doing it, with Claude as my guide, not from a textbook. That means some of what’s below may be wrong or oversimplified, and I’m fine with that risk as long as I get what I came for: to understand my tools, get better at virtual photography and grow my Instagram channel along the way. I’ve marked what I measured or computed myself and what Claude explained to me. If you spot a mistake, or you know a better way to look at something, please tell me in the comments.

You can play with every number in this article. The small widgets do the real math, and every number in the text was recomputed in code, not copied from a chat.

Key takeaways:

  • An RGB triple is meaningless until you know its color space. A color space fixes three things: which red, green and blue (the primaries), what white is, and how stored numbers map to light.
  • A color space’s gamut is a triangle on the map of visible color. Nothing a screen mixes from three lights can leave it.
  • Same numbers, different color. Pure sRGB red written in Display P3 numbers is #EA3323, not #FF0000. Read the numbers in the wrong space and your colors go dull or oversaturated.
  • Bits give resolution, primaries give range. More bits cut the same colors into finer steps. They never reach a color the primaries can’t make.

What is a color space? Why is it called sRGB?

Here’s where my mental model broke. I had always imagined 255 · 0 · 0 as “red”. But a number can’t be a color on its own. It is an instruction: “drive the red channel to full.” What you see depends on what the red light in your screen actually is. A color space is the contract that pins down what the numbers mean. It fixes three things:

  1. The primaries: exactly which red, green and blue, as measurable points. “Full red” means a specific, physical red.
  2. The white point: what (1, 1, 1) looks like. Most spaces use D65, a standardized daylight (a color temperature of about 6500 K).
  3. The transfer function: how stored numbers map to amounts of light. This is the 2.2 “gamma” from Exposure vs Brightness: a stored 0.5 is only about 21% of the light, not 50%. I’m not going to repeat that here, but it is the third clause of the contract.

So “RGB” on its own is a family. sRGB, Display P3 and BT.2020 are members of it, each with specific values filled in.

The “s” in sRGB stands for standard. It was proposed by HP and Microsoft in 1996 and became IEC 61966-2-1 in 1999. Its primaries are the same as the ones in HDTV (BT.709), based on what typical monitors of the day could show. Nearly everything on the web assumes it: an image with no color information is treated as sRGB.

A map of color, and the triangles on it

Here’s the second thing that blew my mind. In 1931 the CIE (the international lighting commission) published a coordinate system for human vision. Plot every color a person can see on a flat chart, with brightness taken out, and you get a horseshoe-shaped region. I explain where that shape comes from in Where the horseshoe comes from. For now just take it as a map.

A screen mixes three lights. Any mix of three points lands inside the triangle they form, so a color space’s gamut is a triangle on this map. Here are the three I’ll keep mentioning:

Interactive illustration (gamut-chart). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

  • sRGB: the small triangle. The internet’s default, and what almost every screen can show.
  • Display P3: wider red and green. It uses the primaries of digital cinema (DCI-P3) with D65 white and sRGB’s curve, and it is what recent iPhones and Macs show. The definition is in Apple’s docs and the ICC registry.
  • BT.2020: red, green and blue corners almost on the edge of the horseshoe, because its primaries are single wavelengths of light (630, 532 and 467 nm). It was built for UHD and HDR video, and few displays reach all of it.

I computed how much of the horseshoe each triangle covers (as a share of its area on this xy chart, using the CIE data). It comes to about 34% for sRGB, 46% for Display P3 and 64% for BT.2020. You’ll see other figures online, since the result depends on how you measure the area, so treat mine as ballpark.

For nerds: the exact primaries

These are the published values; I use them in the widgets. White is D65 at (0.3127, 0.3290) in all three.

Space Red (x, y) Green (x, y) Blue (x, y)
sRGB (0.640, 0.330) (0.300, 0.600) (0.150, 0.060)
Display P3 (0.680, 0.320) (0.265, 0.690) (0.150, 0.060)
BT.2020 (0.708, 0.292) (0.170, 0.797) (0.131, 0.046)

Same numbers, different color

This is where it gets practical. Take pure sRGB red, 255 · 0 · 0. Written in Display P3 numbers, it is #EA3323 (0.917, 0.200, 0.139). And P3’s own 255 · 0 · 0 is a red that sRGB cannot show at all: in linear light it would need a negative amount of green and blue.

So the same three numbers are two different colors:

Interactive illustration (srgb-vs-p3). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

If your screen is wide-gamut (most recent iPhones and Macs), the second swatch is visibly more vivid. If it isn’t, the widget tells you so, because there’s nothing to see.

This explains the “washed out” and “oversaturated” bugs everyone runs into when a color tag is wrong:

  • sRGB numbers read as P3: every color gets stretched outward. Oversaturated, sunburnt skin.
  • P3 numbers read as sRGB: every color gets pulled inward. Dull and flat.

Profile vs space

A small point that confused me. The color space is the contract (primaries, white, curve). An ICC profile is a small file embedded in an image, or describing a device, that says which contract applies. The system reads the image’s profile and your monitor’s profile and converts between them, so what you meant is what you see.

The screenshots I work with are JPG and PNG files from my PS5. They carry no HDR information and no profile at all, so sRGB is implied: every viewer silently assumes it, and that is what I should be grading for.

Why isn’t more bits enough?

At this point I asked the most engineer question of the whole journey: if sRGB can’t make P3’s red, why not just give each channel more bits? Instead of 256 levels of red, 65,536. Surely more precision covers everything.

It doesn’t, and the reason helped everything click. Bits give resolution, not range. They are two independent things.

For nerds: the ADC analogy

This is how Claude explained it to me, in terms I know from electronics.

A 24-bit analog-to-digital converter with a 0 to 3.3 V reference can resolve microvolts, but it can’t measure 5 V. Bit depth is the resolution; the reference voltage sets the full scale.

In RGB, the primaries are the reference. (1, 0, 0) means “the red emitter at full power”, and that red has a fixed physical spectrum. 8 bits gives you 256 steps between off and that red. 16 bits gives you 65,536 steps between off and the same red.

Here is that in pictures. Every dot is one color you can make by mixing the three primaries in whole steps (equal steps of light, plotted on the same map). First, more bits with the same primaries:

Interactive illustration (dot-grid). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

More bits, denser dots, the exact same triangle. Now the opposite: the same number of steps, but moving the primaries outward:

Interactive illustration (dot-grid). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Same dots, bigger triangle, so each step is coarser. Two different knobs:

Choice What it controls Example
Primaries Range: how big the triangle is sRGB → P3 → BT.2020
Bit depth Resolution: how fine the steps are inside it 8 → 10 → 16-bit

That second picture also hints at a catch. 8 bits gives 256 steps per channel regardless of the triangle, so a bigger triangle spreads the same steps further apart, and you can get banding in smooth gradients. That is why wide gamut and HDR are paired with 10-bit.

Why the triangle is a hard wall

A pixel is three lights added together. Any non-negative mix of three points stays inside the triangle they form, like a weighted average. To reach outside, you would need a negative amount of one light. Negative light doesn’t exist.

For nerds: the twist, you can write down colors outside the triangle

Claude explained this to me, and I recomputed the numbers.

I said you can’t reach outside the triangle, but I was half right. With negative numbers (and values above 1), the sRGB primaries can describe any color mathematically. The greenest P3 green, P3 (0, 1, 0), in linear sRGB coordinates is:

(−0.225, 1.042, −0.079)

Formats built for this exist, such as scRGB and Apple’s “extended sRGB”, which use floating-point values. So unbounded floats solve storage. They don’t solve display: no screen can emit −0.225 red.

The real reason for the contract is that numbers eventually drive specific physical lights, and those differ between devices. A color space defines the numbers relative to known primaries, so software can convert them to this screen’s primaries and clip what doesn’t fit.

What I took away

I used to think an RGB number was a color. It turned out to be an instruction, and a meaningless one without a contract: the primaries define a triangle on a map of visible color, and no number of bits gets you out of that triangle.

What I do differently now: before I worry about a color, I ask what space it is in. For my own work the gamut ceiling that matters isn’t some theoretical limit, it is my screen (P3) and Instagram (effectively sRGB for most viewers).

But this leaves a question I couldn’t stop thinking about. Why is the map that shape? Why a horseshoe, why a curved edge, and why three lights? In Where the horseshoe comes from I go after that.

Did I get something wrong, or do you think about color spaces differently? The comments are open.

frontmatter.title: What an RGB number actually means
frontmatter.description: An RGB number is an instruction, not a color. Color spaces, gamuts, why the same numbers look different on different screens, and why more bits don't help.
